items.title: Nirvana is not heaven — it is the cessation of craving
items.claim: How does Buddhism understand nirvana (nibbana in Pali)?

options.text: The 'blowing out' of the fires of greed, hatred and delusion — the end of suffering and rebirth, attainable in this life as well as at death (parinirvana)
A meditative trance state achieved daily

items.reveal:
The Pali 'nibbana' / Sanskrit 'nirvana' literally means 'blowing out' — as a flame is extinguished. The image is from the Adittapariyaya Sutta (Fire Sermon).

Nirvana attained in life is sometimes distinguished from parinirvana — the full nirvana at death of an enlightened being. The Buddha attained nirvana under the Bodhi tree (around age 35) and parinirvana around age 80.

The Buddha refused to speculate about nirvana's metaphysical status — whether the enlightened being exists, doesn't exist, both or neither after death (Aggi-Vacchagotta Sutta). Speculation does not lead to liberation.
items.why: Translating nirvana as 'heaven' imports Christian assumptions. The Buddhist concept is structurally different — not a destination but an end, not a reward but a release.

items.title: Buddhism has no creator god
items.claim: Does Buddhism teach the existence of a supreme creator deity?

options.text: Yes, the Buddha is the supreme deity worshipped as such
No — classical Buddhism rejects an eternal creator god; gods (devas) may exist but are themselves caught in samsara
Yes, Brahma is the Buddhist supreme being
Only Mahayana Buddhism affirms a creator god

items.reveal:
In the Pali Canon, the Buddha refuses metaphysical speculation about a creator (e.g. the Aggi-Vacchagotta Sutta, the 'parable of the poisoned arrow'). Devas exist but are impermanent and themselves seek liberation. The path to nibbana does not depend on grace from a supreme being.

Later traditions (Pure Land, some Mahayana schools) develop devotional practice toward Buddhas and bodhisattvas, but these are still not creators in the Abrahamic sense.

The Buddha is not a god — he is an awakened human teacher.
items.why: Western religious frameworks define 'religion' through theism. Buddhism is a major world tradition that fits awkwardly inside that frame — and forces a rethink of what 'religion' even means.

items.title: The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible

options.text: The first five books — Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy — traditionally attributed to Moses; also called the Pentateuch or Chumash; the first section of the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh)

items.reveal:
The Hebrew Bible (Tanakh) is structured in three sections: Torah (Teaching, 5 books), Nevi'im (Prophets, 8 books in Jewish count), Ketuvim (Writings, 11 books). 'Tanakh' is an acronym of those three.

The Torah is read in synagogue in an annual cycle (some Reform congregations use a triennial cycle). The cycle ends and restarts on Simchat Torah.

The Written Torah is complemented by the Oral Torah — the rabbinic tradition codified in the Mishnah (around 200 CE) and Talmud (around 500 CE). For Orthodox Judaism, both were revealed at Sinai.
items.why: 'The Torah' is often used loosely. Students need to distinguish Torah (5 books) from Tanakh (24 books) from Talmud (rabbinic commentary) — and notice that the Christian Old Testament has the same content but in different order.
